options.text: A response that only occurs during sleep
A slow, carefully considered response to a stimulus
A voluntary movement controlled by the brain
A rapid, automatic response that does not involve conscious thought

questions.explanation: A reflex is a rapid, involuntary (automatic) response to a stimulus that does not involve conscious thought. Reflexes are protective, allowing the body to respond quickly to potentially dangerous situations.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of components in a reflex arc?

options.text: Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector
Effector, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, receptor
Receptor, motor neurone, relay neurone, sensory neurone, effector
Receptor, relay neurone, sensory neurone, motor neurone, effector

questions.explanation: The correct pathway is: receptor detects stimulus, sensory neurone carries impulse to CNS, relay neurone passes it on within the CNS, motor neurone carries impulse to the effector, which carries out the response.

questions.stem: Why are reflexes faster than voluntary responses?

options.text: Because they only involve motor neurones
Because they do not use synapses
Because they bypass the conscious part of the brain and are coordinated by the spinal cord
Because they use thicker neurones

questions.explanation: Reflexes are coordinated by the spinal cord (or brain stem), not the conscious part of the brain. This shorter pathway with fewer synapses means the response is much faster than if the brain had to process the information consciously.

questions.stem: In the withdrawal reflex, what type of effector pulls your hand away from a hot object?

options.text: A relay neurone
A receptor
A gland
A muscle

questions.explanation: In the withdrawal reflex, the effector is a muscle in the arm that contracts to pull the hand away from the painful stimulus. Effectors can be muscles (which contract) or glands (which secrete), and in this case it is a muscle.

questions.stem: What happens at the synapse between the sensory neurone and relay neurone in a reflex arc?

options.text: Neurotransmitters are released and diffuse across to trigger a new impulse
The electrical impulse jumps directly across the gap
Blood carries hormones from one neurone to the next
The impulse reverses direction and travels backwards

questions.explanation: At the synapse, the arriving impulse causes neurotransmitter chemicals to be released from vesicles. These diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a protective reflex?

options.text: Deciding to pick up a pencil
The pupil constricting in bright light
Walking to school in the morning
Choosing what to eat for lunch

questions.explanation: The pupil reflex is an automatic, protective response where the pupil constricts in bright light to prevent damage to the retina. The other options are voluntary actions that involve conscious decision-making by the brain.

questions.stem: Where are relay neurones located in a reflex arc?

options.text: In the muscles
In the sense organs
In the peripheral nerves
In the spinal cord or brain

questions.explanation: Relay neurones are found within the central nervous system (spinal cord or brain). In a spinal reflex, the relay neurone in the spinal cord connects the sensory neurone to the motor neurone, enabling a rapid response.
